title_en: Shanghai Puxin Investment Management Consulting Co., Ltd. v. BOC International Securities Co., Ltd. — dispute over compensation for property damage
ruling_gist_en: A third party obligated to assist the court in taking preservation measures who maliciously infringes upon the creditor's rights of the preservation applicant, refuses to assist in preservation, or takes other measures to obstruct preservation, resulting in the inability to enforce the final judgment document and causing damage to the applicant because the applicant's creditor's rights cannot be realized, shall bear tort liability for damages to the applicant.

full_text_en:
**Shanghai Puxin Investment Management Consulting Co., Ltd. v. BOCI Securities Co., Ltd. — dispute over property damage compensation**

**Ruling Summary**

A third party who is obligated to assist the court in taking preservation measures and who maliciously infringes upon the creditor’s rights of the preservation applicant, refuses to assist in preservation, or takes other actions that obstruct preservation, resulting in the inability to enforce a final judgment or order and causing damage to the applicant due to the inability to realize its creditor’s rights, shall bear tort liability for damages to the applicant.

Plaintiff: Shanghai Puxin Investment Management Consulting Co., Ltd., domiciled at North Pusong North Road, Changning District, Shanghai.

Legal representative: Ji Wen, Chairman of the Board of the company.

Defendant: BOCI Securities Co., Ltd., domiciled at Yincheng Middle Road, Shanghai.

Legal representative: Xu Gang, Chairman of the Board of the company.

The plaintiff, Shanghai Puxin Investment Management Consulting Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Puxin Company), filed a lawsuit with the Xuhui District People’s Court of Shanghai against the defendant, BOCI Securities Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as BOCI Securities), regarding a dispute over property damage compensation.

**Plaintiff’s Allegations**

During the trial of a case in which the plaintiff sued the co-defendants in another case, Shanghai Jiaheng Industrial Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Jiaheng Company), Shenzhen Weimeite Information Consulting Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Weimeite Company), and Shanghai Tengwu Enterprise Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Tengwu Company), concerning a dispute over an entrustment contract, the enforcement judge, upon the plaintiff’s application, went to the BOCI Securities business department designated by Weimeite Company for securities trading on May 21, 2004, to inquire about and freeze the stocks under 151 shareholder accounts under the company’s fund account. At that time, the defendant believed that it also held a creditor’s right against Weimeite Company. Therefore, the defendant, knowing that Weimeite Company’s fund account actually existed but had simply changed its name to “Tang Jing”, falsely claimed that the business department had no account under that company’s name. When the judge presented five shareholder accounts subordinated under Weimeite Company’s name, the defendant again made excuses and refused to assist in the freeze. On the morning of May 24, without the consent of Weimeite Company, the defendant privately and successively transferred 5.49 million shares of “Zhongfang Real Estate” under Tang Jing’s name to various business departments of BOCI Securities in other regions to evade preservation, resulting in the First Intermediate People’s Court of Shanghai only freezing the five shareholder accounts under Tang Jing’s name. On the 26th of the same month, the judge again went to BOCI Securities to handle the freezing procedures for the remaining 146 shareholder accounts under Tang Jing’s name. BOCI Securities again requested the court to go to its business departments in other regions to handle the procedures. In fact, BOCI Securities had already unilaterally transferred the 143 shareholder accounts under Tang Jing’s name from business departments in other regions to the Shanghai Ouyang Road Securities Business Department of BOCI Securities and also filed a lawsuit against Weimeite Company with the Second Intermediate People’s Court of Shanghai (hereinafter referred to as the Second Intermediate Court) and applied for property preservation. On the same day, the Second Intermediate Court froze the relevant accounts at the Shanghai Ouyang Road Business Department. On June 3, the dispute between the plaintiff and the co-defendants in another case, Jiaheng Company, Weimeite Company, and Tengwu Company, was concluded by mediation. The defendant Jiaheng Company was to pay the plaintiff RMB (hereinafter the same currency) 62.2 million and bear acceptance fees of RMB 321,010 and preservation fees of RMB 300,520. After the mediation document took effect, the plaintiff received a total of RMB 40,181,600 from enforcement proceeds, while the remaining balance of RMB 22,639,930 has never been satisfied. Therefore, the plaintiff filed this lawsuit, requesting the court to order the defendant to compensate the plaintiff for the market value of 5.38 million shares of “Zhongfang Real Estate” as of June 7, 2004, amounting to RMB 19,045,200, and interest losses calculated based on that amount from June 7, 2004, to the effective date of the judgment at the benchmark loan interest rate of the People’s Bank of China for the corresponding period.

**Defendant’s Defense**

The defendant argued that its actions did not constitute infringement, and that the plaintiff Puxin Company’s own gross negligence in the process of applying for preservation was the reason for its failure to successfully freeze the funds. The defendant disagreed with the plaintiff’s claims.

**Facts Found by the Court at First Instance**

The Xuhui District People’s Court of Shanghai found at first instance:

On May 11, 2004, Weimeite Company issued a statement to the Guangyuan West Road Securities Business Department of BOCI Securities, applying to change the account holder name of its fund account to “Tang Jing” and declaring that the assets under that account belonged to it. On the 20th of that month, the First Intermediate Court issued a ruling in the case of Puxin Company v. Jiaheng Company, Weimeite Company, and Tengwu Company, freezing the securities and funds under the 151 shareholder accounts originally opened by Weimeite Company at various securities business departments of BOCI Securities. On the 21st of that month, the enforcement judge of the First Intermediate Court went to the Shanghai Guangyuan West Road Securities Business Department of BOCI Securities, the designated securities trading location of Weimeite Company, to inquire about and freeze the relevant stocks and fund account balances, and provided five shareholder accounts as leads for the inquiry. While submitting the inquiry introduction letter to BOCI Securities, the enforcement judge also served a civil ruling sealing and freezing property worth RMB 62.2 million belonging to Jiaheng Company, Weimeite Company, and Tengwu Company. However, BOCI Securities informed the enforcement judge that if they needed to print account materials, they would need to go to the headquarters of BOCI Securities to handle the relevant inquiry approval procedures. Therefore, on that day, BOCI Securities did not carry out the freeze measures with the First Intermediate Court. On the morning of the 24th of that month, without the consent of Weimeite Company, BOCI Securities unilaterally and successively transferred the designated trading of 5,491,089 shares of “Zhongfang Real Estate” under 146 shareholder accounts in Tang Jing’s name from the Shanghai Guangyuan West Road Business Department of BOCI Securities to four business departments of BOCI Securities in Mudanjiang, Tianjin, Wuhan, and Chongqing, leaving only 235,242 shares of “Zhongfang Real Estate” under the five shareholder accounts provided by the First Intermediate Court on the 21st. On the afternoon of the 24th, the First Intermediate Court served on BOCI Securities the assistance execution notice and civil ruling for freezing all stocks, other securities, and fund balances (stocks: 5.72 million shares of “Zhongfang Real Estate”) under Tang Jing’s fund account opened at the Shanghai Guangyuan West Road Business Department of BOCI Securities. BOCI Securities then assisted the First Intermediate Court in freezing 235,242 shares of “Zhongfang Real Estate” in the five shareholder accounts remaining at the Guangyuan West Road Business Department. On the morning of the 26th of that month, the First Intermediate Court again went to the headquarters of BOCI Securities to handle the freeze procedures for the remaining 146 shareholder accounts under Tang Jing’s name and again served relevant assistance execution notices and civil rulings on BOCI Securities. BOCI Securities again requested the First Intermediate Court to go to its four business departments in Mudanjiang, Tianjin, Wuhan, and Chongqing to handle the procedures and stated that Weimeite Company’s stocks had been pledged to BOCI Securities and that if the court wanted to freeze the stocks, it should go to the business department. The First Intermediate Court then required BOCI Securities to file a record of this matter and inform the First Intermediate Court if any other court froze the stocks under these 151 shareholder accounts in the future. On the same day, without the consent of Weimeite Company, BOCI Securities again unilaterally transferred the designated trading of 143 shareholder accounts under Tang Jing’s name (note: total stocks in these accounts were 5,380,719 shares of “Zhongfang Real Estate”) from the four business departments in Mudanjiang, Tianjin, Wuhan, and Chongqing to the Shanghai Ouyang Road Business Department of BOCI Securities, leaving only three shareholder accounts in Tianjin and Wuhan (note: total stocks under these three accounts were 110,370 shares of “Zhongfang Real Estate”). At that time, the Second Intermediate Court also issued a ruling on that day in the case of BOCI Securities v. Jiaheng Company and Weimeite Company concerning a dispute over an entrustment contract, freezing the bank deposits of Jiaheng Company and Weimeite Company in the amount of RMB 54,559,050 or sealing up equivalent property and rights. BOCI Securities immediately completed the freeze procedures for the disputed 5,380,719 shares of “Zhongfang Real Estate” for the Second Intermediate Court.

On June 3, 2004, the First Intermediate Court issued Civil Mediation Document No. (2004) Hu Yi Zhong Min San (Shang) Chu Zi No. 144 in the case of Puxin Company v. Jiaheng Company, Weimeite Company, and Tengwu Company concerning a dispute over an entrustment contract, confirming that Jiaheng Company would pay Puxin Company RMB 60 million and interest of RMB 2.2 million on the 7th of that month, and that acceptance fees totaling RMB 621,530 would also be borne by Jiaheng Company, with Weimeite Company and Tengwu Company assuming joint and several guaranty liability for Jiaheng Company’s above debts. On the 21st of that month, the First Intermediate Court issued Civil Enforcement Ruling No. (2004) Hu Yi Zhong Zhi Zi No. 417 based on the above civil mediation document, freezing and deducting the bank deposits of the judgment debtors Jiaheng Company, Weimeite Company, and Tengwu Company in the amount of RMB 62,886,332 and corresponding interest. On August 16 of that year, the First Intermediate Court sent an official letter to the Shanghai Guangyuan West Road Business Department of BOCI Securities, requesting it to correct its erroneous actions and to seal up the stocks held by Weimeite Company. On the 17th of that month, BOCI Securities replied to the First Intermediate Court, stating that it had not failed to assist the court in handling the sealing procedures according to regulations. On September 9 of that year, Dongfang Securities Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Dongfang Securities) submitted an application for change of enforcement party, stating that Puxin Company had transferred the entire creditor’s rights under the above civil mediation document to Dongfang Securities, and accordingly applied to change the enforcement applicant to Dongfang Securities. However, this application was not granted by the First Intermediate Court.

In April 2005, the Second Intermediate Court issued a judgment in the case of BOCI Securities v. Jiaheng Company, Weimeite Company, et al., concerning a dispute over an entrustment contract, ruling that Weimeite Company was not liable to BOCI Securities. After this case was concluded by the second instance, Weimeite Company was still not liable to BOCI Securities. On October 28 of that year, the Lanzhou Railway Public Security Bureau handled the sequential freezing procedures for the disputed stocks at the Shanghai Ouyang Road Securities Business Department of BOCI Securities. In November of that year, the First Intermediate Court issued a ruling, suspending the enforcement of Civil Mediation Document No. (2004) Hu Yi Zhong Min San (Shang) Chu Zi No. 144. As of that time, Puxin Company had received a total of RMB 40,181,666.41 from enforcement proceeds in that case, while the remaining balance of RMB 22,639,863.59 has never been satisfied. In May 2007, the disputed stocks were transferred by the Lanzhou Railway Public Security Bureau, which had previously implemented sequential freezing, to the Lanzhou Railway Transport Intermediate Court for processing. On June 13, 2011, Dongfang Securities issued a letter to Puxin Company, rescinding the “Assignment of Creditor’s Rights Agreement” between the two parties and clarifying that the remaining RMB 22,639,930 should be recovered by Puxin Company through legal means on its own. Puxin Company replied in agreement. On October 20 of that year, Puxin Company filed this lawsuit.

**Issue in Dispute**

The issue in dispute in this case was: whether BOCI Securities’ act of transferring securities and obstructing the court’s property preservation measures infringed upon the creditor’s rights that the preservation applicant, Puxin Company, held against the party subject to preservation. Whether Puxin Company could claim tort liability for damages from BOCI Securities under the Tort Liability Law for the damage to its creditor’s rights.

**Opinion of the Court at First Instance**

The Xuhui District People’s Court of Shanghai held at first instance:

BOCI Securities, knowing that Puxin Company had already implemented property preservation against Weimeite Company through the First Intermediate Court, unilaterally and illegally transferred Weimeite Company’s property by changing the designated trading method without Weimeite Company’s consent, causing most of the preservation measures taken by the court against Puxin Company’s creditor’s rights to fail and ultimately resulting in Puxin Company’s litigation creditor’s rights not being fully satisfied. BOCI Securities’ above act of transferring property showed obvious subjective malice, and the causal relationship between this act and the losses incurred by Puxin Company due to the non-satisfaction of its creditor’s rights was also quite clear. Therefore, the fact that BOCI Securities infringed upon Puxin Company’s rights was established. Given that Puxin Company bore no fault for the losses in dispute, BOCI Securities should compensate Puxin Company for all losses caused by the infringement. Now that Puxin Company claims that BOCI Securities should calculate the compensation amount based on the market value of the disputed stocks on the payment date determined by the effective civil mediation document and the starting date for calculating interest losses accordingly, this claim was supported. Although the number of transferred stocks found by the court was slightly larger than the amount claimed by Puxin Company, according to the principle of no trial without complaint, this case did not address the portion of excess stocks.

Accordingly, the Xuhui District People’s Court of Shanghai, based on Article 6, Paragraph 1, and Article 15, Paragraph 1, Item (6) of the Tort Liability Law of the PRC, rendered the following judgment: BOCI Securities shall, within ten days after the judgment takes effect, compensate Puxin Company RMB 19,045,200, and shall also compensate Puxin Company for interest losses on the above amount from June 7, 2004, to the effective date of the judgment at the one-year benchmark loan interest rate announced by the People’s Bank of China for the corresponding period. The case acceptance fee of RMB 185,088.42 shall be borne by BOCI Securities.

After the first-instance judgment, both BOCI Securities and Puxin Company were dissatisfied and appealed to the First Intermediate Court. BOCI Securities argued that the first-instance judgment’s factual determination that BOCI Securities’ actions constituted infringement was erroneous; it did not constitute infringement, and there was no causal relationship between its actions and the damage suffered by Puxin Company. Therefore, it requested the reversal of the original judgment and a new judgment dismissing all of Puxin Company’s first-instance claims. Puxin Company argued that the first-instance judgment was correct but that the interest calculation rate was erroneous, and requested a modification ordering BOCI Securities to compensate Puxin Company for interest losses based on the benchmark loan interest rate announced by the People’s Bank of China for the corresponding period.

**Facts Found by the Court at Second Instance**

The First Intermediate Court, after the second instance, confirmed the facts found at first instance.

**Opinion of the Court at Second Instance**

The First Intermediate Court held at second instance: Puxin Company’s claim seeking tort liability for damages from BOCI Securities presupposes that Puxin Company has rights protected under the Tort Liability Law of the PRC. Article 2, Paragraph 2 of that Law provides: “For the purposes of this Law, civil rights and interests include rights in personam and rights in rem such as the right to life, the right to health, the right to name, the right to reputation, the right to honor, the right to portrait, the right to privacy, the right to marital autonomy, the right to guardianship, the right of ownership, the right to usufruct, the right to security, copyright, patent rights, the exclusive right to use a trademark, the right of discovery, shareholder’s rights, and the right of inheritance.” In this case, Puxin Company filed this lawsuit because it could not obtain satisfaction from Weimeite Company. What was actually damaged was Puxin Company’s creditor’s right against Weimeite Company. The creditor’s right is not specifically listed in the aforementioned legal provision. As to whether it falls under “rights in rem” referred to in that provision — in other words, whether creditor’s rights are within the scope of protection of tort law — this court at second instance held that tort law aims to reconcile and balance the interests of compensating the victim’s losses and the freedom of action of the general public, achieving a unified balance among victim protection, maintaining general social freedom of action, and deterring illegal conduct. Because tort law requires a person to exercise a general duty of care toward the rights of all others in society, regardless of whether there is any legal relationship between the actor and those others, the rights protected by law for those others must, in principle, be absolute rights (such as ownership, personality rights), i.e., rights whose existence can be known by the general public. However, a creditor’s right is a relative right between the creditor and debtor and is not easily known to outsiders. If outsiders were required to exercise a duty of care toward the protection of creditor’s rights, they would inevitably suffer unforeseeable damage, and the general public would be overly constrained in their freedom of action due to their inability to foresee the consequences of their actions, resulting in an imbalance in the legal interests of victim protection and general social freedom of action. Therefore, creditor’s rights should not be protected to the same degree as absolute rights. However, creditor’s rights are not completely excluded from the scope of protection of tort law. If an actor knows of the existence or possible existence of another’s creditor’s right and maliciously infringes upon it, there is no risk of suffering unforeseeable damage as mentioned above. In such circumstances, only by holding the actor liable for tort damages for the harmful consequences it actively pursued can the institutional function of tort law in balancing legal interests be realized, protecting lawful rights and interests and deterring illegal conduct.

In this case, after receiving the preservation notice and relevant civil ruling from the First Intermediate Court, BOCI Securities was already aware of Puxin Company’s possible creditor’s right against Weimeite Company. However, not only did it refuse to assist in handling the preservation procedures, but it also, without Weimeite Company’s consent, transferred the securities from the Shanghai Guangyuan West Road Business Department to four locations across the country and required the enforcement judge to go to those locations to handle the preservation procedures. This clearly demonstrated an intention to transfer property and obstruct the court’s preservation measures. Furthermore, considering that in the case BOCI Securities filed against Weimeite Company at the Second Intermediate Court, immediately after the Second Intermediate Court approved the preservation upon BOCI Securities’ application, BOCI Securities transferred most of the securities back from the aforementioned four locations to the Shanghai Ouyang Road Business Department and completed the preservation procedures with the Second Intermediate Court on the same day, it can be sufficiently established that BOCI Securities, acting out of its own interests, maliciously obstructed Puxin Company’s preservation application, which had priority, and used illegal means to compete for the order of property preservation. Its malice in infringing upon Puxin Company’s lawful rights and interests was extremely obvious. Based on the above analysis, BOCI Securities engaged in malicious infringement of Puxin Company’s creditor’s rights, and Puxin Company is entitled to seek protection under the Tort Liability Law for the damage to its creditor’s rights.

BOCI Securities further argued that there was no causal relationship between its actions and the damage to Puxin Company’s creditor’s rights. In this regard, this court at second instance held that for a causal relationship to be established in the sense of tort law, two requirements must be met simultaneously: first, if the act had not occurred, the damage would not have arisen; second, according to general social perception, if the act occurs, such damage would ordinarily result. Examining this case, on the one hand, if BOCI Securities had assisted the First Intermediate Court in preservation, Puxin Company’s creditor’s rights would not have been unsatisfied. On the other hand, according to general social perception, BOCI Securities’ obstruction of preservation was sufficient to cause the debtor to transfer and conceal property or to cause such property to be preserved by other right holders, among other situations that jeopardize the creditor’s realization of its rights. In this case, it was precisely after Puxin Company’s preservation attempts failed that Weimeite Company’s securities were sequentially sealed up by others, ultimately causing damage to Puxin Company. In summary, there was a causal relationship in the sense of tort law between BOCI Securities’ actions and the damage suffered by Puxin Company. Therefore, BOCI Securities’ argument on this point was not accepted.

Based on the foregoing, the first-instance judgment ordering BOCI Securities to bear tort liability for damages to Puxin Company was not improper, and BOCI Securities’ grounds for appeal could not be sustained.

As for Puxin Company’s grounds for appeal, this court at second instance held that the first-instance court’s support of Puxin Company’s claim for interest compensation based on the one-year benchmark loan interest rate announced by the People’s Bank of China for the corresponding period was not improper. Puxin Company’s request on appeal to change the method of calculating interest lacked legal and contractual basis and was not accepted by this court at second instance.

In conclusion, the first instance correctly found the facts, applied the law correctly, and followed proper procedures. The First Intermediate Court, pursuant to Article 153, Paragraph 1, Item (1) and Article 158 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, rendered the following judgment:

Appeal dismissed; the original judgment is affirmed.

The second-instance case acceptance fee for the appeal filed by the appellant Puxin Company, RMB 12,341.77, shall be borne by Puxin Company. The second-instance case acceptance fee for the appeal filed by the appellant BOCI Securities, RMB 185,088.42, shall be borne by BOCI Securities.

This judgment is the final judgment.
